nameStory: The Hubei Anemone gets its name from Hubei Province in China, where this beautiful flowering plant naturally grows. In Chinese, it's charmingly called 'broken bowl flower' (dǎpòwǎnhuāhuā), though no one knows exactly why - perhaps the delicate petals reminded someone of porcelain fragments scattered on the ground.
description: Hubei Anemone is a graceful perennial flower that belongs to the buttercup family, though it looks nothing like the sunny yellow buttercups you might know. This Asian native produces elegant pink or white flowers that bloom in late summer and fall when most other flowers are fading. The plant forms neat clumps and can spread slowly through underground runners, making it a popular choice for gardeners who want late-season color.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Delicate 5-petaled flowers in soft pink or white, about 2 inches across, with a prominent cluster of yellow stamens in the center that feel slightly fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Dark green leaves divided into three leaflets with toothed edges, arranged alternately on the stem and feeling slightly rough and textured when rubbed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright clumps 1-3 feet tall with slender, branching flower stems that sway gently in the breeze above the foliage mound

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces fluffy, cotton-like seed heads after flowering that catch the light and feel soft and silky when touched

habitat: In New England, Hubei Anemone is found almost exclusively in cultivated gardens, particularly in partly shaded borders and woodland garden settings. It prefers rich, well-drained soil and thrives in the dappled light under deciduous trees. With only one recorded observation in our region, it remains quite rare in the wild here.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the ground as small, divided leaves that unfurl from the soil in a distinctive three-part pattern.
seasonality.summer: The plant builds its leafy clump and begins sending up tall flower stalks in late summer, with buds forming at the tips.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming season arrives with masses of pink or white flowers, followed by the distinctive fluffy seed heads that persist into late fall.
seasonality.winter: The plant dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no visible trace above ground until spring returns.

funFact: This elegant flower is part of a group commonly called 'Japanese anemones' in garden centers, but most of them actually come from China - it's one of horticulture's most persistent geographical mix-ups!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other fall-blooming anemones sold as 'Japanese anemones,' but true identification requires checking the specific leaf shape and flower timing. Look for the three-parted leaves and late summer to fall blooming period to distinguish it from spring anemones.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Japanese anemone' in most garden centers and nurseries, this plant and its close relatives are actually native to China, not Japan. This naming confusion is so widespread in horticulture that even experienced gardeners often don't realize the true origin of their 'Japanese' anemones.
compareHints: Since this is the only fall-blooming anemone (Eriocapitella) recorded in our New England dataset, compare it with spring-blooming wood anemones (Anemone species) which are much smaller, bloom in early spring, and have white flowers with 6-8 petals instead of 5. The Hubei Anemone is much taller and more robust than our native spring anemones.
